guide.title: Unit 9: Concession, rebuttal, and style in complex arguments: review guide
guide.intro: The final unit brings everything together: arguments that engage opposing views strategically and use word choice and description to persuade. You'll practice recognizing and writing concessions, rebuttals, and refutations.

sections.title: Concession, rebuttal, and refutation
body: A concession grants that part of an opposing view is valid. A rebuttal answers it by explaining why the writer's position still holds. A refutation shows that the opposing claim is false or unsupported.
Strategic concessions build credibility: granting a minor point can make the audience more willing to accept the main one.
points: Concede what is true; rebut what still matters.
Refute with evidence, not with insults.

sections.title: Writing concessions and rebuttals
body: A useful pattern: state the opposing view fairly, grant what is reasonable, then explain why your claim still stands (“Although…, …”; “It is true that…; however…”).
Place the strongest objection where readers will expect it to be answered, usually right after you present your main reasons.
points: Represent the opposing view in terms its supporters would accept.
End the paragraph on your position, not the opponent's.

sections.title: Stylistic choices in a complex argument
body: Word choice and description shape an argument's force: precise, concrete details help readers see what is at stake, and a consistent tone keeps the writer credible.
In complex arguments, style can signal fairness (measured diction when presenting opponents) and urgency (vivid description of consequences).
points: Concrete details persuade more than abstractions.
Avoid loaded words when describing opposing views.

example.prompt: Write a concession and rebuttal for the claim “The town should keep the old courthouse” against the objection “Repairs would be expensive.”
example.solution: “Restoring the courthouse would cost more than demolishing it, at least at first. But a restored building can house offices the town now rents elsewhere, and over twenty years that rent would exceed the repair bill.”

misconceptions: “A concession means giving up your position.”
It grants part of an opposing view while keeping your claim.
A rebuttal explains why your view still holds; a refutation shows the other claim is false.
Description supports evidence; it doesn't substitute for it.

passages.title: Passage 1: The four-day school week
text: (1) Supporters of a four-day school week point to real savings. Districts that have tried it report lower costs for buses, heating, and substitute teachers, and some say teachers are easier to recruit.

(2) Those savings are real, and in a district struggling to fill classrooms, they matter. But the fifth day does not disappear for families. Parents who work five days must find care for that day, and the students least likely to have a supervised, enriching Friday are the ones who most need school.

(3) Nor is it true, as some supporters claim, that longer school days make up for the lost day. The added minutes come at the end of the afternoon, when attention is lowest, and the research on whether achievement holds steady is mixed at best.
(4) A district may still choose four days. If it does, it should fund the fifth day for the families who cannot.
passages.attribution: Written for StudySprint by its editors. It describes reported experiences with four-day weeks in general terms.

passages.title: Passage 2: The Grover Street mill
text: (1) The mill on Grover Street has been empty for thirty years. Its windows are broken, pigeons nest in the loading bays, and the developer who bought it last spring says it would be cheaper to tear down than to repair.

(2) He is right about the cost. But walk inside on a winter afternoon, when the low sun comes through what is left of the glass and lights the long brick floor, and you will see what the town would lose: the room where three generations of its workers made blankets that warmed the country.
(3) Other towns have turned buildings like this into apartments, shops, and studios that draw visitors for decades. A wrecking ball is cheaper this year. It is not cheaper forever.

passages.title: Draft 1: A student paragraph about a later curfew
text: The following is a draft of a student's paragraph. It may need revision.

(1) The town's 10 p.m. curfew for teenagers should be moved to 11 p.m. on weekends. (2) Many school events, such as concerts and games, end after 9:30. (3) Some residents worry that a later curfew would increase noise and vandalism. (4) Those people are wrong. (5) A later curfew would let students attend events and get home legally.

passages.title: Draft 2: A student paragraph about saving a neighborhood pool
text: The following is a draft of a student's paragraph. It may need revision.
(1) The city plans to close the Westside pool. (2) The pool is a place. (3) In summer, hundreds of kids use it. (4) The city says the pool costs too much to operate. (5) Closing it would be bad.

questions.prompt: In paragraph 2, the sentence “Those savings are real, and in a district struggling to fill classrooms, they matter” is best described as
choices: an anecdote
the thesis
a concession
a refutation
questions.explanation: The writer grants that the supporters' point about savings is valid.
choiceExplanations: The thesis comes later; this grants an opposing point.
A refutation would show the claim is false.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the sentence that begins “But the fifth day does not disappear for families”?
choices: To summarize the research
To rebut the supporters' argument by raising a cost the savings don't account for
To agree fully with supporters
To describe a school bus
questions.explanation: After conceding the savings, the writer explains why they don't settle the question.
choiceExplanations: Buses were mentioned earlier as a saving.

questions.prompt: How does paragraph 3 differ from paragraph 2 in how it responds to supporters?
choices: Both paragraphs agree with supporters
Paragraph 3 concedes, while paragraph 2 refutes
Paragraph 3 refutes a specific claim as unsupported, while paragraph 2 concedes a point and then rebuts it
Paragraph 3 introduces the supporters' view for the first time
questions.explanation: “Nor is it true…” challenges the claim that longer days compensate; paragraph 2 grants savings before answering.

questions.prompt: How does the conclusion (paragraph 4) reflect the complexity of the argument?
choices: It abandons the writer's concerns
It introduces an unrelated topic
It insists that no district should ever use four days
It allows that a district may still choose four days but adds a condition that addresses the writer's main concern
questions.explanation: Rather than an absolute ban, the writer qualifies the position with a practical condition.
choiceExplanations: The condition answers the concern about families.
The conclusion explicitly allows the choice.

questions.prompt: In paragraph 2, “He is right about the cost” functions as
choices: a concession to the developer's point
a description of the mill
a refutation of the developer's point
the passage's conclusion
questions.explanation: The writer grants that demolition is cheaper before turning to what would be lost.
choiceExplanations: This sentence grants a point; the description follows.
The writer agrees with this part.

questions.prompt: What is the main effect of the description of the winter sun on the brick floor?
choices: It proves that repairs would be cheap
It describes the developer's plans
It shows that the building is dangerous
It helps readers see the building's beauty and history, making its loss feel concrete
questions.explanation: Vivid, specific imagery shows what the town would lose.
choiceExplanations: The developer's plans aren't described here.
The description is admiring, not about danger.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer describe the broken windows and nesting pigeons in paragraph 1?
choices: To describe the town's wildlife
To present the building's poor condition honestly before arguing for it
To show that the developer is dishonest
To argue that the building should be torn down
questions.explanation: Admitting the decay up front makes the later argument more credible.
choiceExplanations: The writer agrees with the developer about cost.

questions.prompt: How do the final two sentences (“A wrecking ball is cheaper this year. It is not cheaper forever.”) answer the developer?
choices: They change the subject to the town's history
They accept his short-term point while rebutting it with a longer view of cost
They agree with him completely
They refute his claim that demolition is cheaper now
questions.explanation: The first grants the present cost; the second rebuts by pointing to long-term value.
choiceExplanations: The first sentence agrees that demolition is cheaper now.

questions.prompt: What is the main problem with sentence (4)?
choices: It concedes too much
It repeats sentence (1)
It dismisses the residents' concern without giving a reason
It provides too much evidence
questions.explanation: Saying “those people are wrong” offers no rebuttal.

questions.prompt: Which revision of sentence (4) best rebuts the concern in sentence (3)?
choices: But the later curfew would apply only on weekends, when most teens out late are coming home from supervised school events.
Those people should mind their own business.
Vandalism happens everywhere.
Noise is sometimes a problem.
questions.explanation: It answers the concern by limiting when the change applies and explaining who would be out.
choiceExplanations: This doesn't connect the concern to the proposal.

questions.prompt: Which sentence, added after sentence (3), would best concede part of the residents' concern?
choices: It is reasonable to expect that some teenagers would misuse the extra hour.
Curfews were invented long ago.
Teenagers never cause problems.
Residents always complain.
questions.explanation: Granting a reasonable point builds credibility before the rebuttal.
choiceExplanations: This is an absolute, easily refuted claim.

questions.prompt: Where should the writer place the response to the residents' concern for the greatest effect?
choices: At the very beginning of the paragraph
Right after the concern is stated, before the paragraph ends on the benefit to students
It shouldn't be included
After sentence (5), as the paragraph's last sentence
questions.explanation: Answering the objection as soon as it's raised, then ending on the writer's position, leaves readers with the claim.
choiceExplanations: Before the concern appears, the response would make no sense.
An unanswered objection weakens the paragraph.
Ending on the objection gives it the last word.

questions.prompt: Sentence (2), “The pool is a place,” is weak because
choices: it contains a rebuttal
it is too detailed
it uses a comparison
it is vague and adds no description or support
questions.explanation: It tells the reader nothing about why the pool matters.

questions.prompt: Which revision of sentence (2) uses description most effectively to support the writer's purpose?
choices: On July afternoons, the pool is the one cool place within walking distance for families in apartments without air conditioning.
The pool is very nice.
The pool is a rectangle of water.
The pool is a public facility owned by the city.
questions.explanation: Specific details show who depends on the pool and why, supporting the argument against closing it.
choiceExplanations: This is accurate but irrelevant to the argument.
This is a neutral fact without persuasive force.

questions.prompt: Sentence (4) presents the city's objection. Which sentence, added after it, best concedes and rebuts?
choices: Money is not important.
The city is lying.
The pool costs a lot.
The pool does cost money to run, but a small summer fee or a sponsor could cover much of that cost without closing it.
questions.explanation: It grants the cost, then offers a reasoned alternative to closure.

questions.prompt: Which revision of sentence (5) best combines precise word choice with the writer's position?
choices: Closing it would be a total catastrophe for the universe.
Closing it would be really, really bad.
Closing the Westside pool would take away a safe, free summer refuge from the families with the fewest alternatives.
Closing it would be a choice.
questions.explanation: Precise words (safe, free, refuge, fewest alternatives) name exactly what would be lost and for whom.
choiceExplanations: Intensifiers add emphasis but no meaning.
